title: Columns with labels
objectives: Build a Series and a DataFrame, and select by label and by position.
Filter rows with a Boolean mask and multiply two columns matched by label.

screens.title: A row by its position
screens.prose:
`.iloc` counts rows by position, from 0, whatever their labels.

```python
print(df.iloc[1]["close"])
```
screens.question: What does it print?

widget.label: Value printed
widget.accept: 12.31: position 1 is the second row, 5 March.

hints.text: Positions start at 0. Which row is position 1?
Position 0 is 4 March, so position 1 is the next row.
Row 5 March, column `close`: 12.31.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count rows from 0, then read the close.

byKey.from-one: 12.55 is the close in row 0, and also the open on 5 March. Position 1 is the second row; read its close.
byKey.third: You counted one row too far. Position 0 is 4 March, so position 1 is 5 March.

explain.text: Positions start at 0, so `iloc[1]` is the second row, 5 March, and its close is 12.31. `iloc[-1]` is the last row, as in a list. The labels play no part.

screens.title: A slice of labels
screens.prose:

screens.question: What does it print?

hints.text: Does this slice stop before its end label, like a list slice?

feedback.correct: Both end labels are included: 3 closes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every row from the first label to the last, both included.

byKey.list-slice: You stopped before the end label, as a list slice does. A label slice includes both ends.
byKey.all: The slice keeps only the rows between the two labels, so 4 and 8 March are out.

explain.text: A `.loc` slice runs from the first label to the last, both included: 5, 6 and 7 March. A position slice works like a list, so `df.iloc[1:3]` gives rows 1 and 2 only.

screens.title: Rows that pass a test
screens.prose:
A mask works inside the square brackets too. Comparing two columns gives one True or False per row.

```python
up = df[df["close"] > df["open"]]
```
screens.question: Tap the date of every row in `up`.

hints.text: For each row, is the close above the open?
Check 5 March: is 12.31 above 12.55?
Close beats open on 4, 6 and 7 March.

feedback.correct: 4, 6 and 7 March closed above their open.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep a row only when its close is above its open.

byKey.down: Those are the days the stock fell. The mask keeps rows where the close is above the open.
byKey.r1c0: On 5 March the close, 12.31, is below the open, 12.55, so the mask is False.
byKey.r4c0: On 8 March the close, 12.44, is below the open, 12.60, so the mask is False.

explain.text: `df["close"] > df["open"]` compares the two columns row by row, matched by date. The mask is True on 4, 6 and 7 March, and those rows survive whole.

screens.title: Label or position
screens.prose:
Everything so far, in one place.

```python
df["close"]                  # one column, a Series
df[["open", "close"]]        # several columns, a DataFrame
df.loc["2024-03-07"]         # a row by its label
df.loc["2024-03-05":"2024-03-07"]   # both ends included
df.iloc[0], df.iloc[-1]      # rows by position
df[df["close"] > df["open"]] # rows where a mask is True
```

explain.text: `df["volume"]` picks the column by name, then `.iloc[-1]` takes its last position: 24300. Labels go with `.loc` and positions with `.iloc`; mixing them fails.

ideas: A DataFrame is a set of labelled columns that share one index; one column with its index is a Series.
`df["close"]` picks a column by name. `.loc` finds rows by label, both slice ends included; `.iloc` by position, like a list.
`df[mask]` keeps the rows where a Boolean mask is True. Column arithmetic is matched row by row on the index.

formula.name: Label or position
formula.note: `.loc` slices keep both ends; `.iloc` slices stop before the end.

summary.trap: `df[0]` does not give the first row: it looks for a column named 0 and raises `KeyError`. Use `df.iloc[0]`.

options.text: A Series holds one type, so a row that mixes columns becomes all decimals
The volume column was stored as decimals all along
options.why: You assumed the column changed. `df["volume"]` still prints whole numbers; only the row copy was converted.

options.text: pandas prints every number to two decimal places
options.why: You assumed a print setting. The decimals appear because the row was converted to one type.
You blamed `.loc`. `df.loc["2024-03-07", "volume"]` alone is the whole number 19800.
